25711-freedom-in-science-and-teaching-fr:
Ernst Haeckel writes this defence of freedom in science and teaching, translated from German with a prefatory note by T. H. Huxley, published in New York by Appleton in 1879. Haeckel replies to Professor Virchow, whose attack on science teaching sparked the controversy.

Huxley, asked to state his own view, recalls Gay's lines on those who interpose in quarrels, and shudders at the hard hitting on both sides. Haeckel argues that teaching must follow evidence, not fear, and that science in schools serves truth and public life. The debate still speaks to classrooms today.
3685-egypt-la-mort-de-philae:
Pierre Loti writes travel sketches of Egypt under the shadow of change, in a book whose title means the death of Philae. The opening chapter, A Winter Midnight Before the Great Sphinx, describes a clear, dreamlike night, with a bright silver moon lighting a world that seems no longer ours, suffused with rosy color. Loti walks among temples that modern dams and tourists threaten.

Philae, the island temple of Isis, was doomed to drowning by the Aswan Dam, and Loti mourns it as a symbol of old Egypt. His prose favors moonlight, silence, and decay over guidebook fact. The book suits readers who love Egypt as a place of feeling, and who want Loti's elegy for a world passing away.
9627-buried-cities-volume-3-mycenae:
Jennie Hall's Buried Cities, Part 3: Mycenae, tells young readers of the bronze-age citadel of legend. Hall opens by asking children if they love to dig for hidden treasure. The book then follows Mycenae's walls, tombs, and bronze finds: helmets, daggers, and brooches pictured from original sources. Captions by a fellow teacher guide the eye.

Stories of kings, graves, and gold give the citadel its Homeric glow, while diggers' patience brings it back to light. Hall writes with clarity and warmth for school use. A reader gets a lively first history of Mycenae, where myth meets the spade.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acoemetae:
Acoemetae, from Greek akoimetai, those who do not rest, is sometimes a general name for Eastern ascetics famed for rigorous vigils. Usually it names a distinct Greek or Basilian monastic order devoted to unceasing prayer and praise, day and night. Alexander, a nobly born man who fled Byzantium's court, founded the order about 400 for the desert, loving solitude and fearing episcopal honours.

Returning to Constantinople to establish the laus perennis, the perpetual praise, he brought experience from his first Euphrates foundation and three hundred monks. Hostility from Patriarch Nestorius and Emperor Theodosius drove him from his monastery, but he finally built Gomon at the mouth of the Black Sea, where he died about 440. His successors founded the great Irenaion monastery, and Studius later founded the famous Studium in the city.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acta-sanctoru:
Acta Sanctorum Hiberniae, the short title of the Franciscan John Colgan's celebrated work on the Irish saints, printed at Louvain in 1645. Its full Latin title runs to the acts of the saints of old and greater Scotland, or Ireland, drawn from manuscripts across Europe and ancient monuments, with notes and appendices. Colgan, born in County Derry in 1592, entered the Irish Franciscan house at Louvain in 1612 and was ordained in 1618.

Aided by Hugh Ward, Stephen White, and Michael O'Cleary, Colgan gathered enormous material for Irish saints' lives. After thirty years of sifting, he put his Acta to press, with part of the cost met by Armagh's Archbishop O'Reilly. The first volume, covering January, February, and March, was meant as volume three of his Ecclesiastical Antiquities of Ireland; only one volume appeared. For students of Irish church history it remains invaluable.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acta-triadis-:
Acta Triadis Thaumaturgae, the Acts of a Wonder-working Triad, gives St. Patrick's, St. Brigid's, and St. Columba's lives. John Colgan published it at Louvain in 1647, largely funded by Thomas Fleming, Archbishop of Dublin. Its full title presents the acts of the three common patrons of old and greater Scotland, or Ireland, gathered from ancient writers, with scholia, commentaries, and appendices.

Lack of funds alone stopped publication of all the priceless material Colgan had transcribed and prepared. The catalogue of manuscripts left in his cell at his death shows he had detailed Irish missionaries' labours across England and Scotland, Belgium and Alsace-Lorraine, Burgundy, Germany, and Italy. Only a small remnant of those unpublished volumes now sits in the Franciscan Library at Merchants' Quay, Dublin. Colgan died at Louvain on 15 January 1658, aged 66.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ad-universali:
Ad Universalis Ecclesiae is a papal constitution of Pius IX, issued on 7 February 1862, on admission to religious orders of men where solemn vows are prescribed. It completes three earlier decrees, Romani Pontifices and Regulari Disciplinae of 1848 and Neminem Latet of 1857. It marks a distinct departure from Tridentine law on the age and other requirements for solemn vows, for old and new orders, congregations, and institutes alike.

Its immediate occasion was settling doubts over solemn vows' validity when Neminem Latet went unobserved, that is, without three years' profession of simple vows. That rule aimed to guard orders from hastily admitting youths with no true vocation. It also barred youths whose lives, morals, and bodily and mental gifts had never been properly investigated, with testimonials from their native bishops. The constitution thus ties admission to a tested vocation and a documented record.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-advocatus-ecc:
Advocatus Ecclesiae is a medieval name for certain lay persons, generally of noble birth. Under given conditions, their duty was representing a particular church or monastery and defending its rights against force. Before secular courts, pleading for their clients specially bound these advocates. Civil jurisdiction in the church or monastery's domain was theirs, and they had to protect the church with arms if actually assaulted.

Finally, advocates led the men-at-arms in the church or monastery's name and commanded them in wartime. In return they received definite revenues from church possessions, in supplies or services, or as a lien on church property. Such advocates appear even in Roman times. A Carthage synod decreed in 401 that the emperor, with the bishops, should provide defensores for churches. Gregory I confined the office to clergy, and under Franks and Carolingians its duties were enlarged and defined.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agapetae:
Agapetae, from agapetai, beloved, were in the first Christian century virgins consecrated to God by a chastity vow, living alongside laymen. At first this spiritual-life community of mutual support, grounded in 1 Corinthians 9:5, was holy and edifying. Later it produced abuses and scandals, so fourth-century councils forbade it.

The association likely began because these virgins, not living in community, needed laymen to manage their material interests, naturally choosing men who, like themselves, had vowed chastity. St. Jerome asked indignantly, after degeneration, whence the plague of Agapetae entered the churches. A letter of St. Cyprian shows such abuses in Africa and the East. The Council of Ancyra in 314 forbade consecrated virgins to live thus with men as sisters. Agapetae was also a Gnostic branch in 395, teaching that pure minds purified relations of the sexes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agnoetae:
Agnoetae, from agnoeo, to be ignorant of, is the name for those who denied the omniscience of God or of Christ. The Theophronians, named for Theophronius of Cappadocia in 370, denied God past knowledge by memory or certain future knowledge. They taught that even for past knowledge he required study and reflection. Arians, holding Christ's nature inferior to his Father's, claimed he was ignorant of many things, citing his words on judgment day and his frequent questions.

Apollinarists, denying Christ a human soul or at least a human intellect, necessarily saw him as devoid of knowledge. Nestorians generally, and Adoptionists renewing their error, believed Christ's knowledge limited, growing as he grew in age. Monophysites logically believed Christ knew all things, having one divine nature, but Severian Monophysites set limits to his knowledge. Luther allowed Christ extraordinary knowledge, while Bucer, Calvin, and Zwingli denied his omniscience.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amphorae:
Clay vessels fitted with handles, amphorae served many household uses in the ancient world, above all holding wine. In Christian Rome they appear in the catacombs. Painted scenes show boats laden with them and a boatman on the Tiber with such a cargo. A dove with an olive branch perches above, a sign of the peace the dead were believed to enjoy.

About sixty of these vessels found in the catacombs carry marks peculiar to Christians, above all the monogram of Christ, sometimes set between palms. One fragment in the Lateran museum reads Vivas in Deo. A fine group comes from the cellar of the house of Saints John and Paul on the Coelian hill, where inscribed pieces link everyday pottery to early Christian burial custom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ampullae:
Small vessels found among the fragments in the Roman catacombs, ampullae take several forms, and telling them apart matters for reading early Christian burial. Some are cups from the funeral banquet. Some held the scented oils buried with the dead, as Jews and pagans also buried such oils. A third class, the so-called blood ampullae, holds a dark red sediment once taken for a martyr's blood.

For a time the presence of such a vessel counted as a mark of a martyr's tomb. But Martigny and then Kraus argued against accepting the blood theory without reserve, and the article weighs their case. It closes with a better attested custom. Ampullae of oil from lamps at famous martyrs' shrines, such as Saint Mennas in Egypt, went home with pilgrims, often stamped with the saint's image.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amyclae:
Amyclae was one of the most ancient towns of Greece, set in a fertile, wooded district quite close to Sparta. It stood not far from the river Eurotas. Homer names it in the Iliad, and legend made it the home of Tyndarus and of Castor and Pollux, the brothers known as the Amyclaei fratres.

In church history it survives as a titular see of the Peloponnesus, in the province of Hellas and suffragan to Corinth. During the Middle Ages it became a Latin see, known to the French rulers of Achaia as Micles or Nicles. It was later united with the sees of Veligosti and Leondari, or Megalopolis.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostolicae-c:
Apostolicae Curae is a bull, a formal papal letter, of Leo XIII dated 15 September 1896. It gives the latest papal decision on the validity of Anglican orders, the ordination of Anglican clergy. Earlier decisions had already ruled such orders invalid, and Catholic practice assumed it, since Anglican clergymen who converted and sought Catholic priesthood were ordained unconditionally, as if never ordained before.

In recent years some Anglican clergy and laity argued that this practice came from poor inquiry and mistaken assumptions, which historical research could no longer sustain. Those hoping for corporate reunion, the return of a whole Anglican body to Rome, pressed the plea hardest. The article sets out Leo's answer to that plea and the reasoning behind a decision that still shapes relations between the two churches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arcae:
Arcae, also called Arca and now Tel-Arka, was a titular see on the Phoenician coast between Tripolis and Antaradus, under Tyre. Its bishops' list runs from 364 to 451 in Gams. It served as a Latin see through the Crusades, and today its title belongs to Greek and Maronite bishops. In antiquity it was famed for Aphrodite's worship and for a temple of Emperor Alexander Severus, whose birth there in a temple occurred during his parents' visit.

It endured long sieges by Arab conquerors in Syria in the seventh century and by Crusaders in 1099, into whose hands it in time fell. Later the Mamelukes destroyed it after they expelled the Christian population. Another Arcae in Cappadocia, under Melitene, has a bishops' list from 431 to 680. The entry compresses a port's pagan, Crusader, and ruined phases.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arsacidae:
The Arsacids, who governed the Persian empire from 256 BC to AD 224, reigned when Christianity first reached the lands watered by the Euphrates and Tigris. Nestorian traditions give no very accurate account of relations between Arsacid kings and Persian Christians. Mari ibn Sulayman calls those relations excellent, with churches enjoying profound peace until the Sassanid Sapor I took power.

Yet the same chronicler, writing of Abraham, an early Persian patriarch, speaks of a persecution in his lifetime, repeated by other chroniclers. It ended by miracle, the chronicler says. The Persian king's son, epileptic or possessed, was healed by Abraham, and the grateful prince ordered Christians protected. The entry weighs a tradition of peace against a tale of persecution and healing, showing how early Persian church history survives in conflicting chronicles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-augilae:
Augilae, also spelled Augila, was a titular see of Cyrenaica in northern Africa, set in an oasis of the Libyan desert. The oasis, still known as Audjelah or Aoudjila, stood as a chief station on the caravan route from Cairo to Fezzan. Its forests of date palms were already famous in the time of Herodotus, and they still crown three small hills rising from unbroken red sand.

The sand nearby is strongly laced with salts of soda, the entry notes. In the author's day the oasis held a Muslim population of about ten thousand, ruled by an official of the Bey of Tripoli. That official drew from the oasis an annual revenue of twelve thousand dollars. The sum marks how much the palm groves and the caravan trade were worth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caesarea-maur:
Caesarea in Mauretania began as Iol, a coastal town where King Bocchus lived, which passed at times to the kings of Numidia. Juba II, on receiving Mauretania from Augustus, made the town his capital and renamed it Caesarea. After his son Ptolemy was deposed, it became capital of the province of Mauretania Caesarea, and under Claudius a Roman colony.

Moors burned it late in the fourth century, Justinian's troops besieged it in 533, and the province soon slipped from Byzantine hands. The French took it in 1840, and it is now Cherchel in Algeria, with Roman ruins nearby and trade in oil, tobacco, and earthenware. Four Catholic bishops of the see and one Donatist are known between 314 and 484.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caesarea-pala:
Caesarea on the Palestinian coast began as Straton's Tower, and Herod renamed it for Augustus, building temples, palaces, a theatre, a port, and great colonnades. From 13 B.C. it served as the civil and military capital of Judaea, home to Roman procurators such as Pilate and Felix. Saint Peter founded its church by baptizing the centurion Cornelius, and Saint Paul stayed there often and spent two years imprisoned there before Rome.

In the third century Origen sought refuge at Caesarea and wrote many works there, among them the Hexapla, and with Saint Pamphilus he built a theological school of wide fame. Its library, counted the richest in antiquity, was likely destroyed by Persians in 614 or Saracens about 637. As metropolis of Palaestina Prima it once counted thirty-two suffragan sees.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-carrhae:
Carrhae, the Haran of the Bible, was a titular see of Mesopotamia named Harranu, or Road, in Assyrian records. It centered the worship of Sin, the moon goddess, among a Sabean people. Abraham came there from Ur in Chaldea, his family stayed while he moved on to Canaan, Rebecca was born there, and Jacob spent fourteen years there with his uncle Laban.

Assyrians took it under Hezekiah, Ezekiel notes its trade with Tyre, and its plain saw Crassus killed by Parthians in 53 B.C. and Galerius beaten in 296. Christianity spread slowly, Julian the Apostate preferred it to Christian Edessa, and under Justinian most people were still heathen, though it later became a suffragan of Edessa. Eleven bishops from the fourth to sixth centuries include Vitus, Protogenes, and Abrahamius, and its sugar-loaf houses and Rebecca's well survive near modern Orfa.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-catenae:
Catenae take their name from the Latin word for a chain. They are collections of passages from Bible commentators, above all the Fathers, linked together verse by verse to give a continuous reading of a scriptural text. They work as anthologies of exegesis. They preserve the literal sense of Scripture from very old manuscripts, some now lost.

Their value goes beyond interpretation. Later compilers gathered what survived of fourth- and fifth-century commentators. As a result, catenae often hold the only remains of important patristic writings. The article traces these compilers, who arose once the great commentators had passed, and lists the manuscripts and printed collections where catenae can be studied.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-clazomenae:
Clazomenae, a titular see of Asia Minor, was founded first on the Ionian Sea's southern shore, about fifteen miles from Smyrna. It ranked among the twelve cities of the Ionian Confederation, reaching its height under Lydian rule. After Croesus's death its people fled the Persians for the island opposite their town, now Saint John's Isle. Alexander the Great joined the island to the mainland by a pier, still used between modern Vourla and the island.

The island Clazomenae gave birth to philosophers Hermotimus and Anaxagoras. Its see was suffragan to Ephesus. Lequien names two bishops: Eusebius of Ephesus (431) and Chalcedon (451), and Macarius of the Eighth Ecumenical Council (869). When Smyrna became a metropolis, Clazomenae passed to it. It returned to Ephesus by Patriarch Nilus's act in 1387. After that date its history leaves no trace, and only the ancient pier remains.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-codex-bezae:
Codex Bezae, also called Codex Cantabrigiensis, ranks among the Greek New Testament's five most important manuscripts, most interesting for its readings. It takes its name from Theodore Beza, Calvin's friend and successor, and from Cambridge University, which received it as his gift in 1581. Written in uncial characters, the quarto volume of vellum measures ten by eight inches, with one column to a page, Greek on the left and Latin facing it on the right.

The codex holds only the Four Gospels, in the order Matthew, John, Luke, Mark, then a few Latin verses of the Third Epistle of Saint John, and the Acts. Much is missing from the original scribe's work, though a tenth-century hand supplied bracketed passages. The gap between Gospels and Acts and the fragment of Third John suggest the Catholic Epistles once stood there, and Jude's absence may point to its omission.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-colossae:
Little survives of Colossae's history, and Sophrone Pétridès's entry gathers what is known. It was a titular see of Phrygia in Asia Minor, suppressed in 1894. Its later name, Colassae, likely keeps the old Phrygian form. Once chief city of southwestern Phrygia, it stood on the trade road from Sardis to Celaenae. It made fine wool, whose color took the name colossinus. Its ruin came from changed roads, nearby Laodicea's founding, and hard earthquakes. It kept municipal freedom, yet Strabo calls it a small town.

Colossae held its own coinage under the empire. Saint Paul, probably about 61, wrote its people an epistle from Rome. They may have learned the faith from him. The city was home to his companions Archippus and Philemon, with Appia, Onesimus, and Epaphras, who likely founded the church there. Later it kept a bishopric, and its site still draws students.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cusae:
A short entry describes Cusae, a titular see of Egypt on the western bank of the Nile. Its Coptic name was Koskos, its Greek forms ranged from Kousos to Kousai, and its Latin forms from Cussa to Cusae. Today it is the fellah town of El-Kousiyet, between the railway stations of Derut and Montfalut.

Nearby stands Deir-el-Moharag, the largest and richest of the seven great Coptic monasteries, where the Holy Family is said to have stayed and pilgrims still gather. The city appears in the Synecdemus of Hierocles and later lists as a suffragan of Antinoe. Lequien names two bishops for the see: Achilles, a Meletian, in 325, and Theonas at Constantinople in 553. It must not be confused with Kysis in the Great Oasis.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dies-irae:
Dies Irae, Latin for Day of Wrath, is the sequence sung in requiem Masses, named from its opening words. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry sets out when the Roman Missal orders it sung, above all at funerals and on All Souls Day. It is also sung at anniversary Masses and on the third, seventh, and thirtieth days after death. In other daily requiem Masses its use is left to the celebrant.

The entry traces the chant through centuries of use, translation, and debate over its author and its plainchant tune. Its verses on judgment day made it one of the best known pieces of Latin sacred song. Readers will find here both the rules for its use and the story of its long fame.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-docetae:
The Docetae were a heretical sect reaching back to apostolic times. Their name comes from a Greek word for appearance, since they taught that Christ only seemed to be a man. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry explains that some denied his human nature wholly, while others denied only his body, his birth, or his death. The name itself, best rendered as Illusionists, first appears in a letter of Serapion of Antioch.

Serapion first allowed the reading of the Gospel of Peter at Rhossos, then banned it when he found the sect behind it. The entry follows the heresy from Marcionist circles to a council at Orleans in 1022, which condemned Catharists for the same denial. It closes by noting the old error revived in modern theosophic and spiritist circles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-erythrae:
Erythrae, a titular see in Asia Minor, began in legend as a colony founded by settlers from Crete. Kings ruled it first, and then it moved through oligarchy and democracy before becoming tributary to Croesus and Cyrus. Athens came next as its master, then Sparta, and at last it won independence. After Alexander it answered to various masters until 191 before Christ, when it took the Roman side while still keeping its autonomy.

Herophile the Sibyl and temples of Hercules, Athena Polias, and more made Erythrae famous. Early on it became a suffragan of Ephesus, counting bishops from Eutychius in 431 to Arsaphius in 868, with Michael in 1229. The see, the city, and the port had all vanished by the sixteenth century. Litri or Rithri, a new village, has risen on its site not far from Tshesmé, and the ruins hold walls, a theatre, aqueducts, columns, and a Byzantine fortress.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fabrica-eccle:
Fabrica Ecclesiae is Latin for the building of a church, but in wider use it means the funds for building, repair, upkeep, and daily worship. The phrase first appears in a letter of Pope Simplicius to Gaudentius of Aufina in 475. In the first Christian centuries, all church temporalities in a diocese formed one common fund at the cathedral.

The bishop spent it on worship, clergy, and the poor. In the fifth century, above all in Italy, that fund split into four parts, one of which went to the fabrica. Sicily in 494 set none aside, Gaul seems not to have known the allotment, and Spain gave a third to the luminare, or lights. As country churches grew, each gained its own patrimony, since donors gave to one church. Owners had to fund upkeep, and patron, benefice holder, and tithe holders shared the burden. Gregory IX's Decretals and Trent fixed this law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hortulus-anim:
Hortulus Animae, or Little Garden of the Soul, was a prayer book hugely popular in Latin and German forms in the early sixteenth century. William Schaffener printed the earliest known edition at Strasburg, dated 13 March 1498. New editions with supplements and changes followed constantly from Strasburg, other German cities, and even Lyons.

Many editions, though small, carried beautifully designed woodcuts. Between 1516 and 1521 alone, eighteen editions carried cuts from Hans Springinklee and Erhard Schön. A German edition earliest of all appeared in 1501, though Latin editions predominate. Like the Hours and Primers familiar in France and England, the Hortulus gives pride of place to the Little Office of Our Lady, with a wider variety of popular prayers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-margaritae:
Margaritae were memory aids for canon lawyers of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. Teachers of canon law commented on Gratian's Decretum and on collections of Decretals, shaping their treatises in many forms and names. Margaritae gathered the weightier propositions, summaries, and axioms to help memory.

They arranged their matter alphabetically or by subject, and some used neat mnemonic verses. A number survive, though not all their authors are known with certainty. Some were printed with the Decretum or Decretals. Several Decretum editions carry a verse Modus legendi, opening with a couplet on what each distinction means, so any reader may see divine and human law. Another, still unpublished and perhaps the Breviarium pauperum in verse, covers the five books of Decretals in metre and ends by vowing to write those five books in verse.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mirabilia-urb:
The Mirabilia Urbis Romae is the name of a medieval Latin guide to Rome from about 1150. Its unknown writer knew little of the city's true past, and mixed real sites with tales and marvels. From the time of Boniface VIII (1294-1303) to that of John XXII (1316-34) the book was reworked and won full trust, though its stock of errors kept growing.

De Rossi first drew note to its varied forms in his Roma Sotterranea. For ages the Mirabilia led pilgrims round Rome, and shaped how they read the old city. Its blend of fact and fancy makes it a key witness to the medieval mind.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-notitia-provi:
The Notitia Provinciarum et Civitatum Africae lists bishops and sees of Latin North Africa province by province. Drawn up when the Vandal king Huneric summoned the episcopate to Carthage on 1 February 484, it runs through Proconsularis, Numidia, Byzacena, both Mauretanias, Tripolitana, and Sardinia.

Naming exiled bishops and vacant sees besides those present, the list stands as a key authority for the African church and its geography under persecution. It survives inside Victor of Vita's history of the Vandal persecution, in whose editions it is printed. Scholars prize it for African church history and for the geography of its provinces.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-o-filii-et-fi:
O filii et filiae, the Easter hymn opening O sons and daughters, celebrates the risen King in twelve short stanzas. Jean Tisserand, a Franciscan preacher who died in 1494, wrote nine stanzas, with three more added early, each closing on the cry Alleluia.

Still beloved in France and spread abroad, the hymn frames the Easter versicle and response in its final stanzas, calling for praise and thanks on the holy feast. Guéranger called it the Joyful Canticle and printed it with a triple Alleluia before and after. Guéranger’s Liturgical Year calls it the Joyful Canticle and prints text with translation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paul-heliae:
Paul Heliae, or Povl Helgesen, was a Danish Carmelite and foe of the Reformation, born at Varberg in Halland about 1480 and dead after 1534, place unknown. Entering his home town's Carmelite convent young, he rose to lecturer on Scripture and bachelor of divinity, was elected provincial in 1519, and soon became professor at Copenhagen University.

In those posts he had to take sides when a Lutheran pastor reached Saint Nicholas parish and a schismatic church code appeared. Preaching at court, he warmly defended Catholic faith and pointedly taxed the king's morals. He had to flee until Christian II's fall and Frederick I's election gave Catholicism brief respite. Misguided zeal then clouded his own orthodoxy. He denounced simony, greed, and clerical vice in Protestant tones. He printed a Danish version of Luther's prayer book, keeping only what matched Catholic faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-serrae:
Serrae, a titular metropolitan see in Macedonia more correctly spelled Serrhae, is the Siris of Herodotus and the Sirae of Livy. Inscriptions give the official spelling as Sirrha. The city, now Sérès in Turkish usage, lies in eastern Macedonia about forty-three miles northeast of Salonica, in the Strymon plain below the mountains. Xerxes left sick followers there on his way back to the Hellespont, and Aemilius Paulus received a deputation from Perseus there after Pydna.

Under Byzantium the city held great strategic weight in wars against Slavs and Bulgars. Bulgars took it in 1206, Emperor John Ducas retook it in 1245, and the Serbian king Stephen Dushan seized it in turn and was crowned there in 1345. A Greek turncoat serving Murad I captured it in 1373. Now capital of a district in the Salonica province, it holds about 30,000 people, of whom 13,000 are Turks by the entry's count.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-summae:
Summae were the compendiums of theology, philosophy, and canon law used as textbooks and reference works in the Middle Ages. This entry weighs rival claims for the first such work. Origen's Peri Archon and Hilary's De Trinitate both have backers, and so does the Speculum Universale of Radulfus Ardens, who wrote in the eleventh century. Wide-ranging works by Isidore and Rabanus also qualify in a broad sense.

In the stricter sense, Summa names the technical systematic works that appeared in the twelfth century, also called Sentences, with Summulae as a later diminutive. Their method came from Gerbert and Abelard's Sic et Non. It set opposing views side by side, then resolved them in order, using reasoned debate for theology as well as philosophy. Peter Hispanus's Summulae Logicales crowned the logical branch.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-supremi-disci:
Supremi disciplinae is the Motu Proprio of Pius X, issued 2 July 1911, on Holy Days of obligation. This entry explains its reform. On such days the faithful owed both Mass attendance and abstention from servile work. Rising living costs and the needs of harvests had already thinned the list in several countries. Pius now extended that thinning to the whole Church for uniformity.

Apart from Sundays, obligation now bound only eight days. They were Christmas, New Year's Day, and Epiphany, plus the Ascension, the Immaculate Conception, the Assumption, Peter and Paul, and All Saints. Where a feast had already been abolished or moved, the new law did not revive it. In the United States, Epiphany and Peter and Paul stayed out. Patronal feasts ceased to bind, though bishops might move their celebration to Sunday.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tacapae:
Tacapae was a titular see of Tripolitana in northern Africa, named Tacapas, Tacapa, or Tacapes on ancient milestones, probably Tacape in Greek. Mentioned in many ancient geographies, its history is otherwise unknown. It lay in fertile country in the interior of Syrtis Minor, served by several roads, and acted as the region's commercial centre.

First attached to Byzantium, it became a Roman colony in the third century within Tripolitana. It still survived under Justinian, who fortified the town. Today it is Gabes, chief town of a civil district and seat of a military command over southern Tunis. It has 1,200 people, 400 of them French, living in an oasis watered by the Wady Gabes. Three bishops are known, from Carthage in 403 and 411, exile in 484, and Carthage again in 525.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tenebrae:
Tenebrae is the service of Matins and Lauds for the last three days of Holy Week. The Caeremoniale Episcoporum directs that it be anticipated, sung after Compline about three on the eve. Benedict XIV explains that Lauds follows Matins at once, ending with the close of day. This signified the Sun of Justice setting and the darkness of his condemners. Originally Matins were sung after midnight, so extinguished lights meant complete darkness.

Putting out lights in the night Office dates probably from the fifth century. Early ordos stress gradual extinction during Friday Matins, while Thursday stayed lit and Saturday lay dark, save one candle by the lectern. Kutschker reads the three days' Office as a funeral dirge for Christ's death. Since Christ lay three days in the tomb, each day repeated the same mourning rites. The entry closes with the later clatter, read as nature's convulsion at his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-testem-benevo:
Testem benevolentiae is an Apostolic Letter of Leo XIII to Cardinal Gibbons, 22 January 1899. It opens by explaining its title: as the pope had praised America's people and Church, so now he names things to avoid or correct, settling injurious controversies. The occasion was the preface to the French Life of Isaac Hecker. Leo proposes to examine opinions there on Christian life.

Those opinions held that, to win converts, the Church should adapt to advanced civilization and relax ancient rigour. This covered rule of life and the deposit of faith, passing over or minimizing doctrine or giving it new meanings. The Vatican Council is clear: faith is no speculative doctrine to be relinquished under any pretext, since that would alienate Catholics. The Church must hold the same doctrine in the same sense and way. Rules of life may change with time, place, or custom, but only by the Church's judgment.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thaenae:
Thaenae was a titular see in Africa Byzacena, a maritime city of Byzacium in Africa Propria. It stood at a river mouth, now Wady Tina, on the Syrtis Minor. Its ruins, Henshir Tina, lie north of Ounca, formerly Junca, in Tunis. A hill crowned by an acropolis topped the city, its walls ran two Roman miles, and it held a large cemetery. The name varies in Greek and Latin writers, but Punic coins give its native name as Tainat.

Under Hadrian or Antoninus it became a colony called Colonia Aelia Augusta Mercurialis Thaenitana. Six bishops are known: Eucratius at Carthage in 256, Latonius at Carthage in 411 against the Donatist Securus, and Peregrinus, once a deacon of St Augustine. Paschasius was exiled by Huneric in 484, Pontianus attended Junca in 525, and Felix signed against the Monothelites in 641. A council met at Thaenae early in the fourth century, with three canons surviving.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thermae-basil:
Cappadocian see Thermae Basilicae, first suffragan of Caesarea, is the small diocese traced here. Greek episcopal lists down to the thirteenth century rank it first among Caesarea's suffragans. A bishop may date from Saint Basil's age; four more are named with certainty across councils and exiles.

Firminius sat at Chalcedon in 451, and Photinus at Constantinople under Patriarch Gennadius in 459. Musonius suffered exile under Justin I about 518, and Theodore attended the Sixth Ecumenical Council in 681 and the Council in Trullo in 692. Hierocles calls the city Therma in Cappadocia Prima under Caesarea. It likely matches Aquae Sarvenae on the road from Tavium to Caesarea, now Terzili Hammam, a village north of Caesarea.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thermopylae:
Pass of Thermopylae, where Leonidas fell, gives this titular see its fame, suffragan of Athens in Achaia Prima. A defile about four miles long, its chief passage barred by a wall Phocidians built against Thessalians in the sixth century before Christ, takes its name from two hot springs. Today they are called Loutra, or the baths. July 480 before Christ saw Leonidas of Sparta fall with 1,300 Spartans and allies against Xerxes's vast army.

Brennus with 170,000 Gauls forced the pass in 279 before Christ. Romans beat Antiochus III there in 191, and Alaric's Goths passed in 395 after Christ to ravage Greece. Justinian restored the walls in the sixth century. Latins made it a diocese after 1204, and Innocent III's letters of 1208 and 1210 to Bishop Arnulfus survive among later bishops' records.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tubunae:
A titular see whose province is disputed, placed in Mauretania Caesariensis by one authority and in Numidia by another, since it stood on the boundary of the two. Some writers speak of two distinct cities, but Müller's view of a single city seems the more plausible, and it was a municipium and frontier post under a praepositus limitis.

St. Augustine and St. Alypius stayed there as guests of Count Boniface, and in 479 Huneric exiled many Catholics thither. Its ruins, known as Tobna in the Department of Constantine, Algeria, cover three successive towns, Roman, Byzantine and Arab, and its bishops include St. Nemesianus, at Carthage in 256.
doe-osti-3013851-pressurized-water-react: PWR aerosols got settled, and this DOE text rates containment settling for accidents. The pages detail the source findings. The reactor folks get their data. The reactor was pressurized water. The data were reactor. The terms were source. The settling was aerosol.
egypt-la-mort-de-philae:
Pierre Loti, a French naval officer and novelist, traveled through Egypt in winter and mourned a country he saw vanishing. W. P. Baines translated the French text, La Mort de Philae, into English. Loti writes in dreamy, rich prose rather than guidebook facts. Temples and tombs matter to him as living presences, not ruins on a route.

Moonlight over the Sphinx and the pyramids opens the book with a shiver of awe. Later chapters wander Cairo's Mameluke tombs, where silence has replaced prayer, and sit inside a crowded Coptic service he calls archaic Christianity. Donkey caravans, tourist bands, and misty Nile mornings pass through his pages. Modern works that shift the river for irrigation draw his anger, since rising water threatens the island temple of Philae. Travel readers who want mood, color, and grief for old Egypt, rather than dates and measurements, find Loti at his most spellbinding here.
khunrath-amphitheatrum-sapientiae-aetern:
Physician Heinrich Khunrath created the Amphitheatrum Sapientiae Aeternae, the Amphitheatre of Eternal Wisdom, printed in 1609. This entry gives the text as a transcription. Khunrath mixed alchemy, prayer, and medicine in one system.

His famous engraved plates join text to image in dense symbols. The prose circles Christ, nature, and the stone of the wise. Readers must move slowly through layers of Latin terms and emblems. The work is a mystic's masterwork of the German Renaissance. Students of hermetic thought prize it as a peak of that art. Few texts reward slow study quite like it.
nasa-tm-19660007964-the-atmosphere-explo:
Edwin Moses at Goddard described the solar array built for the Atmosphere Explorer-B satellite in this October 1965 report. The array's job, the catalog note says, was to recharge the satellite's silver-zinc batteries. Solar cells make power only in sunlight. Batteries carry the spacecraft through each pass in Earth's shadow, then refill on the Sun side.

Atmosphere Explorer-B was sent to study the upper air. Its instruments needed steady power through thousands of orbits. Moses presents the array as a designed system, not a loose set of panels. Reports like this one record the power engineering that kept small science satellites alive and working.
nasa-tm-19690023911-research-achievement:
Aerophysics research at Marshall fills volume 3 of the center's Research Achievements Review, in a 1968 memorandum, TM X-53799. Aerophysics studies how air flows around rockets and what forces that flow creates. The opening study treats external flow around rockets flying at high angles of attack, comparing facility tests against analytical predictions of normal force.

John W. Davis then reports Ludwieg tube pilot tests and high Reynolds number test equipment. The volume's record also lists shock tunnel simulation, jet exhaust flow studies, and wind velocity measurement work. A human auditory response model appears among the topics as well. Together the pieces survey how Marshall tested and calculated the air loads its rockets would meet.
podcast-dannyjones-CkUDwq_-6AE:
Former covert CIA officer Andrew Bustamante speaks freely with Danny Jones in this visit. Bustamante served seven years in the agency and fought as an Air Force veteran. He now teaches spy craft to the public.

Jones gives him room to tell tales from years spent in disguise. Bustamante explains how officers gather facts while living a cover life. He shares lessons on reading people and staying calm under watch. The episode is a broad, uncensored tour of an operative's world, from recruit training to life after the agency. Every tale comes with a lesson attached.
podcast-dannyjones-Hz8jLmCSCaE:
Rizwan Virk is a computer scientist and investor who wrote a popular book on the simulation hypothesis, the idea that our reality is computed. On Danny Jones's podcast, he argues that ancient religious texts describe the same idea centuries early, confirming the hypothesis from an unexpected direction.

Virk reads Hindu and other sacred writings beside modern computing, finding simulated worlds, avatars, and resets in both. Jones follows the parallels and asks where analogy ends and evidence begins. The argument is Virk's synthesis, not a scholarly consensus, and it is preserved as his presentation. Listeners enjoy the double vision the episode trains: scripture as software documentation, physics as theology. Whether the match is profound or coincidental is the question the conversation leaves open on purpose.
podcast-dannyjones-UCXE6KdMYaE:
Harvard astronomer Avi Loeb has argued that the interstellar object called 3I/ATLAS might be artificial, like Oumuamua before it. He joins Danny Jones to warn that NASA is hiding what it knows about the visitor. Loeb presents his reading of the object's anomalies and his case for treating alien technology as a live hypothesis.

Loeb's standing makes the argument unavoidable: a department chair turned Galileo Project founder, publishing and data-gathering in the open. His colleagues largely read the same objects as comets, and the dispute plays out here in Loeb's telling. Jones asks what the images show and what they withhold. The episode preserves the most prominent scientific dissent in modern astronomy at full length, useful for any listener deciding where bold inference ends and promotion begins.
podcast-joerogan-Bfo2xIeaOAE:
Noland Arbaugh, the first person to receive a Neuralink brain implant, talks with Joe Rogan in episode 2167. Arbaugh was paralyzed in a diving accident before joining Elon Musk's brain-chip trial. The device lets him move a computer cursor with thought alone.

Arbaugh describes daily life with the chip, from playing games to the surgery and its setbacks. He explains what it feels like when thought becomes action on a screen. Rogan asks about the future of the tech for both healing and enhancement. Future-minded listeners hear the first human account of living with a brain implant.
podcast-tuckercarlson-jvbd6HAziaE:
Tucker Carlson opens with dread about a looming global war. A drone strike on Moscow by Ukraine killed Russian civilians. He turns to retired Colonel Doug Macgregor for answers.

Macgregor says Russians doubt American sincerity on ending the war. He still credits Trump with a true wish for peace. The title shifts to cartel weapons and border risk. Macgregor argues cartels now pose a bigger threat than Russia. The episode pairs a war update with a warning that the closest danger may sit just south of home. His answers stay cool while the topics burn.
